name: Retainers
lead: Orthodontic retainers are custom-made appliances worn after braces or clear aligners to hold teeth in their new, straighter positions. They protect the result people paid for: a straight, even smile and well-aligned front teeth are among the most visible parts of the lower face, and without retention teeth tend to drift back toward their old positions, a process called relapse.[1][4]

Relapse is attributed to several forces: elastic recoil of the gum and periodontal fibers, pressure from the lips, cheeks and tongue, the way the upper and lower teeth meet, and continued growth and ageing changes in the jaws.[1][4] Retainers hold the teeth still while the surrounding tissues adapt to the new arrangement. The main designs are the Hawley retainer (a wire and acrylic palate plate), clear vacuum-formed retainers, and fixed retainers bonded behind the front teeth.[1][3]

A 2023 Cochrane review of 47 randomized trials with 4,377 participants compared retainer types and wear regimes and concluded that the certainty of the evidence was low to very low, so it could not rank one approach above another.[5] Clinical reviews describe retention as potentially lifelong, and the length of wear is set by the treating orthodontist.[4]

In looksmaxxing forums retainers come up less as a cosmetic product than as a side issue in jaw-development discussions: users ask whether wearing retainers interferes with mewing, palate expansion or forward jaw growth, and whether to keep teeth stable before jaw surgery.[15][16][17][18] These are questions posed by community members; no published study has tested them.

angle.text: Retainers keep the tooth alignment achieved with braces or aligners from shifting back, so the straighter smile and even front teeth people sought remain. Fixed wires and clear night-time trays are the usual ways of keeping the result.

paras: A Hawley retainer has a metal bow running across the front teeth, usually with two adjustment loops, set into an acrylic plate that sits against the palate. It is among the oldest removable designs and is named for Charles A. Hawley. Reported advantages are rigidity, adjustability and ease of construction; reported drawbacks are visibility, effects on speech, fracture risk, and weaker control of the lower front teeth than vacuum-formed designs.[1] A modification called Astics replaces the front wire with a clear one, and other variants such as the Wrap Around extend the wire further back.[1][3]

Vacuum-formed retainers (VFRs) are clear plastic shells, made of polypropylene or similar material, that cover the whole arch or sit as a clip-on from canine to canine. They are nearly invisible, easy to fabricate and widely prescribed, and are usually worn overnight.[1][3] Dentists commonly refer to them by trade names such as Essix, Zendura and Vivera.[2]

Fixed retainers are lengths of wire bonded with composite to the tongue-side surfaces of the front teeth, either a multistranded wire across all six front teeth or a plain wire on the canines only. They depend less on patient cooperation and are used where relapse is more likely, such as after correcting severe rotations or closing a gap between the upper central incisors, but they are harder to clean.[1]

Less common designs include the Begg retainer, whose bow wraps behind the last molar so that the teeth can settle into the bite and which can be worn while eating, and the Barrer spring retainer, which has acrylic on both sides of the front teeth and can correct slight relapse of the lower incisors.[1] A smart-case design pairs a retainer case with a phone app that tracks and rewards wear.[1] Acrylic (polymethyl methacrylate) is the standard material for removable plates, and its use in prosthodontics and retainer making has been reviewed.[10] A 2023 clinical article described 3D metal-printed retainers.[13]

Modern orthodontics took shape in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, with Edward Angle's malocclusion classification and appliances, and the American Journal of Orthodontics was founded in 1915.[2] Retention has been part of that tradition from the start, since corrected teeth were observed to move back after appliances were removed.

Fixed retainers became practical once bonding adhesives replaced the metal bands wrapped around each tooth, a change that took place in the mid-1970s.[2] Clinical experience with direct-bonded retainers, wires attached straight to the teeth with composite, was reported in the American Journal of Orthodontics in 1977.[11] A 1985 article in the Journal of Clinical Orthodontics described what it called invisible retainers, an early step toward the clear removable trays now common.[12]

Large randomized comparisons arrived later. A trial at an orthodontic practice in Bristol, published in 2007, randomized 397 patients to Hawley or vacuum-formed retainers; the Cochrane Collaboration first published its review of retention methods in 2004 and has updated it since.[5][7]

A review in the Australian Dental Journal states that orthodontists cannot predict which patients will relapse or by how much, so clinicians are advised to treat everyone as having a high potential to relapse, and long-term retention is advocated. The same review notes that teeth can also move with normal age changes, and that there is insufficient high-quality evidence on the best retainer type or regime.[4]

A Wikipedia summary of orthodontics states that more than half of patients show some reversion within ten years and that after braces a common pattern is full-time wear for about six months followed by night-time wear for many years.[2] Wear schedules in practice vary by clinic; the orthodontist treating the patient sets them.[1]
A review in the journal Children describes retention as something that should be planned before treatment starts and explained to the patient, who is responsible for following the guidance.[3]

The 2023 Cochrane review assessed randomized trials of retainers and related procedures after braces, excluding aligner studies. Most of the 47 included studies were at high risk of bias. At 12 months, part-time removable retainers were associated with more discomfort but fewer failures and better gum health than fixed retainers, with no clinically meaningful difference in stability. Full-time removable retainers showed no clinically meaningful stability advantage over fixed ones and failed more often. CAD/CAM nitinol and fiber-reinforced fixed retainers gave slightly better stability that did not reach clinical significance, and fiber-reinforced retainers failed earlier by 24 months. Clear plastic and Hawley retainers had similar stability, with Hawley failing less often but rated less comfortable. Part-time and full-time Hawley wear did not differ. The authors rated certainty as low to very low and said they could not draw firm conclusions about any one approach.[5]

A multicenter randomized trial of 35 post-orthodontic patients compared a modified vacuum-formed retainer with palatal coverage against a Hawley retainer, measuring dental cast arch width at debond and at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months. Arch width did not differ between groups at any time point, and patients rated fit, speech, hygiene, durability and comfort similarly; the vacuum-formed design scored higher for appearance.[6]

The Bristol trial of 397 patients over six months found vacuum-formed retainers more cost-effective than Hawley retainers from the perspectives of the health service, the practice and the patient. Most participants preferred them and they broke less often.[7]

A single-center randomized trial of 27 patients treated for bimaxillary proclination (protruding front teeth in both jaws) compared fixed bonded, vacuum-formed and combined retention over 12 months. All three groups showed small changes that the authors judged clinically insignificant; upper incisor inclination differed by about 3.3 degrees between the single-retainer groups and the dual group, leading the authors to suggest dual retention gives better control in these cases.[9]

A qualitative study from Queen Mary University of London interviewed 15 people who had worn vacuum-formed retainers for at least four years. Reported adherence was high early on, motivated by wanting to keep the orthodontic result, and typically declined over time as retainers affected daily life and practical problems arose. Social support helped in both the short and long term; some participants held beliefs that played down the importance of wearing them, and missed follow-up appointments led others to stop. The authors identified six influences on long-term adherence.[8]

Reported problems include decay and gum inflammation when a retainer is worn during eating or put in right after a meal or sugary drink, or when it is poorly cleaned, with fixed retainers harder to keep clean. Vacuum-formed retainers can break in people who grind their teeth, Hawley retainers can alter speech sounds such as d, s and t, particularly in full-time wear, and hot water can warp removable plastic.[1] Brushing with a non-abrasive paste and storing the retainer dry are the cleaning measures described in reference sources.[1]

Fixed retainers have been compared for effects on the supporting gum tissue: a randomized trial examined multistranded wire against fiber-reinforced composite retainers and their effects on the periodontium.[14] Retainers also carry an indirect risk when not worn: relapse, which can undo the alignment achieved.[4]

Retainers appear on looksmax.org mainly in threads that tie them to jaw-growth theories. One poster who had clear aligners at about age 11 or 12 wrote that years in a retainer sized for a younger child may have left the upper jaw behind the lower and that he had stopped wearing it and added mewing and chewing.[15] Other threads ask directly whether retainers stop or reduce palate growth in teenagers, whether a night-time retainer reverses daytime tongue posture progress, and whether to keep or remove retainers after treatment.[16][17][24]

A second strand concerns surgical and expansion plans. Posters planning bimaxillary surgery or a MARPE (miniscrew-assisted palatal expansion) describe wearing retainers to stop their teeth shifting beforehand, and one thread asks how mewing alongside retainers might affect the lower jaw.[18][19][20] Another thread title proposes a myofunctional appliance as an alternative to conventional retainers.[21] Others discuss how retainers interact with mewing and expansion in general terms.[22][23]

Orthodontic references describe retainers as holding tooth position and do not address palatal or maxillary growth.[1][3] Practitioners of mewing and similar approaches argue from the opposite direction, that tongue posture and chewing shape jaw development; those claims and the retainer questions remain untested together.
No studies found on retainers and facial or palatal growth. Clinical research on retainers concerns tooth stability, breakage, comfort, hygiene and cost, summarized above.[5][6][7][9]

timeline.event: The American Journal of Orthodontics is founded, as modern orthodontics consolidates.[2]
Bonding adhesives replace metal bands on each tooth, making bonded brackets and fixed retainers practical.[2]
Clinical experience with direct-bonded orthodontic retainers is reported in the American Journal of Orthodontics.[11]
The Journal of Clinical Orthodontics publishes a report on invisible retainers.[12]
The first Cochrane review of retention procedures after orthodontic braces is published; it is updated in 2016 and 2023.[5]
A randomized trial in Bristol of 397 patients finds vacuum-formed retainers more cost-effective than Hawley retainers.[7]
A qualitative study of long-term vacuum-formed retainer wearers identifies influences on adherence.[8]
A multicenter trial reports similar arch-width retention at 24 months for modified vacuum-formed and Hawley retainers.[6]
The updated Cochrane review includes 47 trials and rates the evidence as low to very low certainty.[5]
A randomized trial compares fixed, vacuum-formed and dual retention after correction of bimaxillary proclination.[9]

lore.intro: Retainer threads on looksmax.org mostly ask whether routine post-braces retainers conflict with mewing, jaw growth or planned expansion surgery.[15][16][17]

claims.claim: Retainers worn through the teen years can stop the palate or maxilla from developing.
claims.believers: Posters describe wearing retainers for several years after treatment and later feeling the upper jaw looked recessed, attributing this to the retainer fixing the arch at its early size.[15][16]
claims.experts: Orthodontic references describe retainers as holding tooth position against relapse and do not describe an effect on palatal or maxillary growth.[1][4] No studies found testing this claim.

claims.claim: Wearing a retainer at night reverses the progress made by mewing during the day.
claims.believers: Forum users ask whether the retainer undoes daytime tongue posture, and some propose skipping retainer nights.[17]
claims.experts: Orthodontic sources describe retainers as maintaining tooth position; no published study has examined their interaction with tongue posture practices.[1]

claims.claim: Retainers are needed to hold teeth stable before or between jaw procedures.
claims.believers: A user planning bimaxillary surgery wrote that he would get night retainers so his teeth would not shift in the meantime.[18]
claims.experts: Retainers are described as preventing relapse after tooth movement, and fixed retainers are used where relapse is more likely.[1] Reviews also note that teeth can shift with ordinary age changes.[4]

claims.claim: Teeth will move back if retainers are stopped, so wear may need to continue indefinitely.
claims.believers: Orthodontists and patients commonly describe retainer wear as a long-term habit to protect the result of treatment.[4]
claims.experts: A clinical review says relapse cannot be predicted for individuals, advocates long-term retention, and notes teeth can also change with age.[4] The Cochrane review could not identify an optimal regime.[5]

claims.claim: A myofunctional appliance or natural oral posture can replace conventional retainers.
claims.believers: One thread title proposes a myofunctional appliance as a method better than retainers.[21]
claims.experts: Reviews of retention cover Hawley, vacuum-formed and fixed designs; no published trial in the reviews cited compares myofunctional approaches with retainers for relapse.[3][5]

claims.claim: Clear vacuum-formed retainers are as effective as Hawley retainers and more pleasant to wear.
claims.believers: Patients who choose clear trays cite their near-invisible look and comfort; in the Bristol trial most participants preferred them.[7]
claims.experts: A 24-month randomized trial found similar arch-width retention with better appearance ratings for the vacuum-formed type, and a Cochrane review found similar stability with Hawley failing less often but being less comfortable.[5][6]

card.summary: Plastic or wire appliances that keep teeth where braces put them; forums debate whether they hold back jaw growth, which nobody has tested.
card.note: Claims that retainers stunt palate growth are untested; wearing instructions come from the treating orthodontist.

quick.overview:
Retainers are worn after braces or aligners to keep teeth from drifting back. Types include Hawley retainers, clear vacuum-formed trays and wires bonded behind the front teeth.

On looksmax.org, some users worry that retainers restrict palate growth or undo mewing. No studies cited here address that.
quick.mechanism: They hold teeth in position while the gum fibers and bone adapt to the new arrangement. Fixed bonded wires work continuously; removable ones depend on being worn.
quick.risks: Reported problems include decay when clear retainers are worn while eating or drinking sugary fluids, plaque and gum inflammation if not cleaned, speech effects from Hawley designs, breakage and warping.
